blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Why ethics matters to a computing professional; the impact of acting ethically or unethically; and the need for copyright legislation.

blocks.heading: Why ethics matters to a computing professional
blocks.text: Ethics is the set of moral principles that guides how a person acts, and a computing professional works where those principles are load-bearing. The law sets a floor - theft, fraud, misuse are crimes - but most of the professional's day sits above that floor: whether to disclose a weakness a client would rather hide, how much care the users' data is owed, whether to ship a system the team doubts. A code of ethics names those choices and sets a standard above the law's floor, which is the first need it answers. The second need is standing. The public meets computing through its professionals, and one misused trust is remembered against all of them, so the profession polices itself before anyone else has to. That is what a professional body is for: the BCS (British Computer Society) and the IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronic Engineers) publish codes of conduct their members agree to follow, so joining one commits the professional to a written standard and signals to employers and clients that here is someone held to it - with the body's guidance to lean on when a decision is hard, which is the third need: hard decisions are lighter with a rule to lean on.

blocks.heading: Acting ethically or unethically: what follows
blocks.text: Every ethical choice in computing lands on three circles: the people the work affects, the client or employer, and the profession. Take the unethical side first, because its chain runs furthest, and its first link is ordinary: most unethical acts in computing begin not with a villain but with a shortcut - the corner cut quietly, the doubt unspoken, the data borrowed ‘just to check’ - which is why a code speaks to ordinary days and not only dramatic ones. A developer copies user data from a client's system: the users' privacy is breached and their trust is broken; the client's confidence collapses and the client warns others; the developer's name and the profession's standing fall together, because the public keeps one memory for all professionals. A house finds a safety flaw in a hospital system and stays silent: the patients carry the risk, the hospital believes in a system that fails, and the profession's word is worth less the next time. The ethical side runs its own chain, and it runs further. Disclosure of the flaw mends it before harm, so the patients are safe, the hospital keeps faith with the house, and the profession's standing is upheld - which is why ethical behaviour is not a cost but an investment: trust is what lets users supply honest data and rely on systems built with care, and trust is spent by the one and earned by the many.

blocks.heading: Why copyright legislation is needed
blocks.text: Software is a work made by someone, and copyright legislation gives that someone the rights of a maker: the legal right to control how the work is copied, adapted and distributed, so a program belongs to its maker unless the right is assigned away, exactly as a book belongs to its author. The need is sharpened by what software is: a work that can be copied exactly, at almost no cost, with no loss to the copy. A novelist's manuscript is safe in a drawer; a finished program can be taken in a moment and shared with the world, so without the right to control copying, a creator's work could be taken and sold by anyone and creating would stop paying - which is the need the law answers. The right holds at every size of maker: a lone developer's program is as much their work as a firm's, and the lone developer has less behind them to absorb the loss, so the law a firm can lean on is the law a lone developer lives by. Two words to keep straight: copyright is the right; plagiarism and copying without permission are acts against it. The legislation earns its keep at both ends of the market it protects: the maker of a popular teaching program and the maker of a niche tool for one clinic both live by the same right to refuse a copy, because the right is what turns making into a living - and the user’s side of the same law is the licence, the maker’s statement of what may be done, which is the next unit’s whole subject.

blocks.heading: Common errors
blocks.text: The recurring slip is defining copyright by its breach. Copyright is the legal right of the creator to control copying and use of their work; copying without permission and plagiarism are acts against that right, not what the right is. The test: is the answer about the right, or about breaking it? The right is copyright; the breach has other names.

blocks.heading: Where this connects
blocks.text: The data whose care these principles govern is the data of 6.1 and 6.2, and the licence terms of the next unit are copyright's practical instruments. The AI that raises the next unit's questions is built on the systems of 3.1 and 4.1, and the whole unit is 8.3's quiet foundation: a database holds people's data only as carefully as the rights and duties of these two sections are honoured.
